before.response:
For this small local dashboard, **SQLite with WAL is a sensible default**. Your recorded decision fits the project’s current scope.

| Tradeoff | SQLite with WAL | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Embedded database; no separate server | Requires a running database service |
| Concurrent access | Readers can run alongside a writer, but writes are serialized | Supports many concurrent readers and writers |
| Operations | Few moving parts; backups must account for WAL state | More administration, with mature backup and recovery tools |
| Deployment | Best when the app and database live on one machine | Works well with multiple app servers and remote clients |
| Features | Enough for typical dashboard queries | Richer permissions, advanced queries, and database tooling |
| Cost | Low resource and maintenance overhead | Higher baseline resource and operational overhead |

WAL improves SQLite’s concurrency, but it still permits only **one writer at a time**. Short transactions usually make that fine for a small dashboard. The database should stay on local storage; WAL is unsuitable for shared network filesystems.

PostgreSQL becomes attractive when you need multiple app instances, frequent simultaneous writes, remote database access, or stronger operational controls. It adds setup and maintenance that a local prototype may not yet benefit from.

I’d keep SQLite WAL now and reconsider if deployment becomes multi-server or measured write contention causes delays. Keep transactions short and use a supported backup method so committed data in the WAL is included.

minimal_same_context.response:
For this small local dashboard, **SQLite with WAL is the better starting point**. PostgreSQL becomes worthwhile when you need multiple application servers, many concurrent writes, or remote database access.

WAL (*write-ahead logging*) lets SQLite readers keep working while a writer updates the database. It improves concurrency, but SQLite still permits only one writer at a time.

| Tradeoff | SQLite with WAL | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Setup and maintenance | Embedded in the app; no database service to manage | Requires a running service, credentials, upgrades, and monitoring |
| Concurrent activity | Good for many reads and brief, occasional writes | Handles many simultaneous writers better |
| Deployment | Well suited to one app on one machine | Well suited to several app instances sharing a database |
| Data features | Supports transactions, constraints, indexes, and common queries | Adds richer types, advanced queries, and database-level access controls |
| Backups | Simple with SQLite’s backup API; copying only the main file during live writes can miss WAL data | Mature backup and recovery tooling, with more operational setup |
| Cost | Very little infrastructure overhead | More memory and administration, or a managed-service bill |

The main SQLite risk is **write contention**. Keep transactions short and configure a busy timeout so brief overlaps can wait instead of failing immediately. WAL also expects processes to share the same machine; avoid putting the database on a network filesystem.

I’d retain the recorded SQLite WAL choice for the prototype. Reconsider PostgreSQL when the dashboard needs multiple hosts, sustained overlapping writes, or centralized access controls. Keep database access isolated in the application so a later migration is manageable, while recognizing that SQL and schema differences will still require work.

after_assembly.response:
For this small local dashboard, **SQLite with WAL is a good starting choice**. PostgreSQL becomes more attractive if you expect multiple app servers or frequent concurrent writes.

| Tradeoff | SQLite with WAL | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Embedded database; no separate server | Requires a running database service |
| Concurrency | Readers can run alongside a writer, but only one writer at a time | Handles many concurrent readers and writers |
| Deployment | Best when the app and database live on one machine | Supports multiple app instances connecting over a network |
| Operations | Few moving parts; backups must account for WAL state | More administration, with mature backup and recovery tools |
| Features | Plenty for dashboard data, filters, and basic reporting | Richer types, permissions, indexing, and advanced queries |

WAL improves SQLite’s concurrency, but long write transactions can still make other writes wait. Keep transactions short and use SQLite’s backup API or another supported backup method instead of copying just the main database file while it is active. WAL also requires processes to share the same host; avoid placing the database on a network filesystem.

Your recorded decision to use SQLite WAL fits the local prototype. Consider PostgreSQL when you need multiple hosts, sustained write concurrency, database-level access controls, or stronger operational recovery options. A small project can need PostgreSQL for those reasons, but size alone doesn’t justify the extra setup.

Three directions for the dashboard’s error page:

1. **Clear recovery:** Explain what failed in plain language, with “Try again” and “Back to dashboard” actions.  
   Acceptance criteria: users understand the problem and can take a useful next step.

2. **Preserve momentum:** Keep the dashboard navigation visible and show any available cached data, marked with its last update time.  
   Acceptance criteria: users can still navigate, and stale data is clearly identified.

3. **Helpful diagnostics:** Show a brief explanation with expandable technical details and a “Copy error details” button.  
   Acceptance criteria: users can share useful troubleshooting information without exposing sensitive data.

I’d start with option 1, then add option 3 for the local prototype. These are proposals; no work has been queued.

minimal_same_context.response:
Three directions for the dashboard’s error page:

1. **Clear and practical:** Explain what failed in plain language, preserve the user’s input, and offer “Try again” and “Back to dashboard.” A good baseline for most errors.

2. **Helpful diagnostics:** Add an expandable “Technical details” section with the error code, timestamp, and a “Copy details” button. Useful when troubleshooting the local prototype.

3. **Keep work moving:** Show which parts of the dashboard still work and offer access to the last saved data, clearly marked with its age. Useful when one failure shouldn’t block everything.

I’d start with option 1 and borrow the expandable details from option 2.

after_assembly.response:
Three directions to explore:

1. **Clear and practical:** Explain what went wrong in plain language, then offer “Try again” and “Back to dashboard.” Include a copyable error ID for troubleshooting.

2. **Helpful context:** Keep the dashboard’s navigation visible and tailor the guidance to the problem. For example: “We couldn’t load your projects. Try refreshing in a moment.”

3. **Warm and reassuring:** Use a simple illustration and friendly copy, with one prominent recovery action. Keep technical details in an expandable section.

For a local prototype, I’d start with option 1: it’s simple to build and makes recovery obvious.
